commit_message:
[Merged] Increase precision for B/W rasterizer.

* src/raster/ftraster.c (Set_High_Precision): Add two more bits to
the precision.  This corrects rendering of some small glyphs, for
example, glyph `xi' in verdana.ttf at 13 ppem.  Testing with ftbench
on my GNU/Linux box I don't see a performance degradation.
pr_title: raster: guard high-precision mode against large bitmap dimensions
pr_description:
The B/W rasterizer's `Set_High_Precision` function selects between two internal coordinate precision modes: a 12-bit mode (4096x scaling) for fine rendering of small glyphs, and a 6-bit mode (64x scaling) for larger content.

Previously, the 12-bit high-precision mode was enabled unconditionally whenever the `FT_OUTLINE_HIGH_PRECISION` flag was set. For large bitmaps, the 64x-per-axis coordinate scaling causes internal arithmetic values to exceed integer bounds, resulting in integer overflow.

This change adds a dimension guard: high precision is only activated when the bitmap's combined top and right extents are less than 256. For larger bitmaps, the rasterizer falls back to the standard 6-bit precision mode, which keeps all intermediate values well within integer range. Small glyph rendering quality (the original motivation for 12-bit precision) is unaffected.

fix_commit_message:
* src/raster/ftraster.c (Set_High_Precision): Limit size.

This should avoid integer overflows:
   https://issues.oss-fuzz.com/issues/490433932
   https://issues.oss-fuzz.com/issues/490464129
agent_reasoning: Without the size check, calling Set_High_Precision with High=1 on a large bitmap unconditionally sets precision_bits=12, causing a 4096x internal coordinate scale. For large bitmaps (e.g., bTop+bRight >= 256), subsequent fixed-point arithmetic in the rasterizer overflows integer types, leading to undefined behavior and potential memory corruption. The fix gates the high-precision path on `ras.bTop + ras.bRight < 256`, ensuring that only small-glyph scenarios — where the scaled coordinates fit safely — use the 12-bit mode. Large bitmaps fall back to the 6-bit mode where the 64x scaling keeps values in range.
